n: A prophecy against Damascus, capital of Syria (Aram), which had allied with Israel against Judah. It will be reduced to a heap of ruins. Assyria captured Damascus in 732 BC.
The towns of Aroer will be abandoned and become pastures where flocks rest undisturbed.

f.g: Here likely a region of towns east of the Jordan controlled by Damascus.

n: Ephraim (northern Israel) will lose its fortresses, and Damascus its kingdom. Syria’s survivors will share the same faded glory as Israel — the two allies fall together.
Israel’s glory will shrink and its strength waste away, like a well-fed body becoming thin.
Israel will be harvested like grain cut by a reaper in the fertile valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem. Most of the people will be taken.

f.g: Grain, such as wheat or barley.
A fertile valley southwest of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:18).

n: Yet a few will be left, like the last olives at the top of a tree after it is shaken. God always preserves a remnant.

f.g: Gathering what is left after harvest (Leviticus 19:10).

f.w: two or three berries in the top

n: In that day people will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel. Judgment will bring them back to God.
They will stop trusting altars and idols made with their own hands, including the Asherah poles and incense altars.

f.g: Asherah poles — wooden symbols of a Canaanite goddess.
Probably incense altars or sun pillars.

n: Israel’s strong cities will be abandoned like the forsaken towns of the Canaanites that fled before Israel long ago.

f.g: The Greek Septuagint reads “the deserted places of the Amorites and Hivites.”

n: Because Israel forgot God its Savior and its Rock, it planted “pleasant plants” and foreign cuttings — likely gardens for pagan fertility gods.

f.g: Possibly gardens of Adonis, a pagan fertility cult.
Foreign cuttings — idolatry imported from other nations.

n: Though they make these gardens sprout quickly, the harvest will vanish in a day of grief and incurable pain.
Isaiah hears the roar of many nations crashing like ocean waves — the armies of Assyria, made up of many peoples.
Though they surge like mighty waters, God will rebuke them, and they will flee like chaff on a hilltop or tumbleweed in a storm.

f.g: Husks blown away on high threshing floors.

n: At evening, terror; by morning, they are gone. This foreshadows the sudden overnight destruction of Sennacherib’s Assyrian army outside Jerusalem.

f.w: before the morning he is not
